title: Hash tables and collision handling
learningObjectives: Explain the concept and its constraints.
Trace the example and reason about its data flow.
Identify complexity, boundary or safety considerations.
Apply the concept in a tested C program.

understand.concept: A hash table maps keys to array positions using a hash function. Different keys can map to the same position, creating a collision. Common collision strategies include separate chaining and open addressing.
understand.whyItMatters: Hash tables can provide efficient average-case lookup, but correctness depends on collision handling, capacity management and a consistent equality rule.
understand.analogy: Treat an algorithm or data structure as a set of operations that must preserve a clearly stated contract.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace formal complexity analysis, C object rules or algorithm preconditions.

explain.narrative:
A hash table maps keys to array positions using a hash function. Different keys can map to the same position, creating a collision. Common collision strategies include separate chaining and open addressing.

Before implementation, state input constraints, empty-case behaviour, ownership and invariants. Compile with warnings and test representative, boundary and failure cases.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.explanation: The function maps an integer to an index within the table when capacity is nonzero. A complete hash table must still resolve collisions and compare full keys.

practise.guidedTask: Give two different keys that collide for a capacity of five.
practise.independentTask: Design a small chained hash table for integer keys and explain insertion, lookup and deletion ownership.
hints: A hash value is not proof that two keys are equal.
The table must handle collisions explicitly.
Resizing changes bucket placement and usually requires rehashing.
